title: About
text: About I’m an AI/ML research engineer and M.Sc. Statistics & Data Science student at LMU Munich (expected graduation: mid-2027). I build and evaluate multimodal models for surgical video in collaboration with ZEISS , and self-supervised systems for archaeological LiDAR. My work combines scalable model training with careful benchmarking and reproducible engineering. I’m interested in reliable medical AI: how models generalize across patients and domains, how uncertainty should shape predictions and human review, and how statistical decision theory can guide model development. I’m looking to pursue these questions through PhD research. I also study agentic systems, with a focus on tool use, evaluation, and failure modes.

title: Kaggriculture — agents for a two-player farming-economy ladder
text: Kaggriculture — agents for a two-player farming-economy ladder Kaggle Featured simulation competition · August – September 2026 · solo · 10,000+ teams Each agent runs a farm for a 720-turn season — hiring hands, planting, raising animals, buying land and selling into a market whose prices react to both players — and whoever banks the most wins. Agents are ranked on a live ladder against everyone else's submissions. I started with my own hierarchical heuristic (perception, pathfinding, an economic value model, task assignment), then learned from public replays that the top of the ladder was running replayed action routes, and moved to route-based agents with my own market-timing layers on top. Most of the work was measurement. I built a paired-seed, both-seats evaluation harness and a validation gate that packages each agent exactly as Kaggle receives it and replays full games through the real loader. I fixed a module-caching bug that had made two "different" agents run identical code, and a tuning script that optimised money when the ladder scores only win or loss. To see what strong opponents actually ran, I crawled the live matchmaking graph and matched their recorded games against local candidates step by step. Climbed from rank 5,852 to 754 in two days in early September, and reached a peak live rating of 2751.5, silver range at the time. Single-constant changes carried most of the gains: one selling order tweak beat its parent 94–26, and a sale-lookahead change beat the strongest public agent 36–4 on fresh seeds. I also showed that a live rating is not a stable measure: byte-identical code scored 2751 one week and 1847 the next, so I stopped comparing ratings across days. title: Full-Corpus Results — Does in-domain SSL improve calibration?
text: For {LeJEPA, DINO v1} × ImageNet ViT-B/16 init, measure zero-shot calibration on HyperKvasir, then repeat after self-supervised pretraining on the complete ~4.9M-image raw GastroNet-5M corpus — all 506 portal archives, streamed directly rather than pre-curated. DINO/ImageNet comes out with zero regressions on accuracy, balanced-accuracy, AUROC or Dice on any task, and is promoted as the resulting foundation-model checkpoint. LMU Munich × ZEISS · standalone benchmark, code public at github.com/DucAnhValentinoNguyen/VLF_Zeiss · earlier 581k-image pilot below Before training, the win condition was fixed in advance (to rule out picking whichever result looks best after the fact): SSL pretraining must not make the model worse, on average, at telling classes apart or segmenting polyps — specifically, no regression on mean balanced-accuracy across the four HyperKvasir classification tasks, or on segmentation Dice, versus the pre-SSL baseline. DINO/ImageNet passes; LeJEPA/ImageNet fails it. DINO's checkpoint is the resulting foundation model, logged as a versioned W&B Artifact for further fine-tuning on other downstream tasks.

title: Full-Corpus Results — The five tasks
text: All five come from HyperKvasir and share the same frozen-feature, weighted-k-NN protocol (k=20 for classification, k=10 for segmentation) — nothing here is a trained classifier head, so every number below is a direct read of how separable the frozen embedding space already is. hkv_findings 20-way | The finest-grained label HyperKvasir has: the specific endoscopic finding in the frame (e.g. a polyp type, an esophagitis grade, a named anatomical landmark). Actually 23 classes in the raw dataset; 3 are dropped for having fewer than 12 labeled images ( hemorrhoids , ileum , ulcerative-colitis-grade-1-2 ), leaving 20. The hardest task — most classes, finest distinctions — and where SSL moves the needle most. 2,196 query images. hkv_category 4-way | A coarser bucket each finding belongs to: anatomical-landmarks, pathological-findings, quality-of-mucosal-views, or therapeutic-interventions. 2,201 query images. hkv_pathology 2-way | Collapses hkv_category further, to the clinically loaded question: is this frame something a clinician should flag ( pathological-findings ), or not (everything else — landmarks, prep-quality shots, therapeutic-intervention frames)? Not the same grouping as "any of the 20 findings" — e.g. cecum , pylorus , z-line (landmarks) and bbps-0-1 / bbps-2-3 (bowel-prep quality) are not pathological. 2,201 query images. hkv_tract 2-way | Upper GI (esophagus/stomach/duodenum, from gastroscopy) vs. lower GI (colon/rectum, from colonoscopy) — a coarse but non-trivial which-procedure question, and already near-saturated pre-SSL (99.4% balanced-accuracy). 2,201 query images. hkv_seg pixel-level | Zero-shot polyp segmentation: dense ViT patch-token features, k-NN label transfer from a 100-image support set, scored by Dice/mIoU against ground-truth masks on 900 held-out frames. The only task that tests where in the frame something is, not just what the frame shows. Two datasets with different levels of certainty. HyperKvasir (the evaluation data) was audited exh

title: Full-Corpus Results — The five tasks
text: austively : every one of its 10,619 images was decoded, hashed and counted. GastroNet-5M (the self-supervised training data, 4,823,974 images) is far too large to decode twice, so its integrity and redundancy were measured on a random sample of 24 of the 493 zip archives (226,256 images, 4.7% of the corpus; seed 0) and extrapolated with uncertainty ranges; the archive and image counts themselves are exact, read from the full manifest. Redundancy is measured with a 64-bit perceptual hash (pHash): two frames are “near-duplicates” if their hashes differ in at most 6 of 64 bits — the same threshold the evaluation split uses, so the two datasets are directly comparable. A pHash match means visually near-identical frames; there are no patient or procedure IDs, so it cannot prove they come from the same procedure.

title: Full-Corpus Results — 3 · HyperKvasir: how unbalanced, and therefore how hard
text: **Images per finding class (all 23 classes, local copy)** Greyed classes are excluded from the benchmark (fewer than 12 images). The largest class has 1,148 images, the smallest kept class 28: an imbalance ratio of 41:1. **Query images per class after de-duplication (20-class findings task)** Red: classes with fewer than 20 query images (6 of 20; the smallest has 6). Per-class accuracy on these is very noisy, so the benchmark reports balanced accuracy over all classes with the caveat that a handful of images can move a class by tens of points. **Share of calibration + query images removed by the near-duplicate filter, per class** The filter is concentrated in three classes: bowel-prep scores ( bbps-2-3 , bbps-0-1 ) and impacted-stool . title: Full-Corpus Results — 4 · GastroNet-5M: what the training stream looks like
text: **Images per archive (all 506 archives, exact)** 363 of 506 archives hold 9.5–10k images; a small number are much smaller (27 archives hold under 8,000 images, together 3.5% of all frames). All 506 are used in every epoch. **Frame size in the sample (8 most common of 2,959 distinct sizes)** Frames are not square and not a fixed size (85% are 512 pixels high, widths vary), stored as RGB PNG (mean 382 KB per frame). The training transform resizes and crops them to the network input; no re-encoding is applied to the stored data. **Brightness of the sampled frames (mean grey level, 0 = black, 255 = white)** Central 90% of frames lie between grey level 73 and 127. Practically no unusable frames: 4 near-black and 1 near-white frame in 226,256; 28 frames are more than half dark pixels (borders, dark views). So blank-filling as a fallback has almost nothing to compensate for. **How redundant is the stream? Distance from each frame to its nearest other frame in the same archive** Red = within 6 bits, i.e. near-duplicate: 7.2% of sampled frames have such a neighbour (HyperKvasir, for comparison, 19.6%). Most frames sit 10–14 bits from their nearest neighbour; a typical frame is genuinely different from every other in its archive. **Near-duplicate rate varies by archive (24 sampled archives, share of frames removable at ≤ 6 bits)** Typical archives have 3.4% (median); archive 0483 has 53%. This heterogeneity is why the corpus-level estimate is a range (3.22–10.62%, bootstrap over archives), not a point.

title: Full-Corpus Results — 5 · What this analysis does not show
text: GastroNet numbers are sample estimates (24 of 493 zip archives); the 13 .7z archives were not sampled, and a whole-archive defect could be missed. The zero-corruption bound assumes frames are independent. No labels, no class balance: GastroNet is unlabelled, so no class or anatomical-site distribution (including the reported upper-GI skew) was measured. Non-endoscopic frames, blur and glare were not detected, only integrity, size, brightness and redundancy. pHash is a proxy: it finds visually near-identical frames, not same-patient frames. Different thresholds give different counts (0.09% at 0 bits, 0.28% at 2, 5.97% at 6 in GastroNet), so the 6-bit figure is a choice, applied identically to both datasets. HyperKvasir has no patient or procedure ID, so splits are image-level; the near-duplicate filter reduces but cannot remove leakage between splits. title: SurgGround — Build Log — What it is
text: At 1 fps a 2-hour procedure is ~7,200 frames — impossible for any vision-language model to see in one pass. The project's spine is fitting a 30–150 minute procedure into a small VLM (InternVL3-2B) at low token cost via a trained TemporalConnector with always-on token reduction, then localizing precisely inside it with a hierarchical-coarse-to-fine or retrieval regime depending on length. Three research bets sit on top of that engineering: abstention-shaped offline RL that penalizes confident wrong answers as much as missed ones, a procedure-graph constraint that makes an impossible phase order unrepresentable, and a clean compression-vs-hierarchy-vs-retrieval comparison across the length range — all trained and evaluated on two owned RTX 4090s, no cluster required. title: SurgGround — Build Log — Real work, not just a plan
text: The first real download of MultiBypass140 on the training box filled a 242 GB disk to zero bytes free and produced not one usable frame. The download script located each surgical centre's videos at a fixed path inside its zip. Real S3 archives from this dataset don't agree on layout — some wrap their contents in an extra directory, some don't — so every "wrapped" zip's ~40–90 GB of video matched no path the script knew to check. It was never extracted to frames, and — since the script only deleted a video after successfully extracting it — never deleted either. It just accumulated, silently, until a disk-full error hit an unattended background job mid-write and the job hung indefinitely. Rewrote the extraction step to search for every directory literally named videos after each zip, wherever it landed, and infer the surgical centre from the matched path itself instead of assuming where it would be. Verified against a synthetic reproduction of both zip layouts, then against the real zip that had triggered the incident — found, extracted, and cleaned up correctly. No real data was lost: the frame output directory on the training GPU was never even touched, since the buggy step never got that far.

title: SurgGround — Build Log — What's next
text: Finish landing all three datasets on the training box, build the frame index, and spot-check parser output against the raw annotations — the actual P1 exit criteria. P3 — zero-shot baselines. Run ≥2 open video-LLMs on grounding, phase segmentation and QA across both the short and long-video regimes. Expected finding: zero-shot grounding on a 2.5-hour procedure is near-random — quantifying that gap is the point. P4 — the first complete result. QLoRA-train the TemporalConnector on the 2B backbone; target ≥10-point grounding improvement over the best zero-shot baseline and a non-trivial number on the 2.5-hour dataset. This alone stands as a result even if nothing after it ships in time. Full technical spec, every design decision, and the day-to-day status log are in the repo.
